newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK's top housing official says supply is the answer.
newsitem.headline: HK's top housing official says supply is the answer.

text.p: Top Hong Kong civil servant for housing Dominic Wong said on Friday the only solution to the territory's soaring property prices was increased supply.
Wong will hold the same post in the Hong Kong administration which takes over after Britain gives up the colony to Communist China on July 1.
"Our belief is...the long term and only solution is to provide more supply," Wong, the Secretary for Housing, told reporters at a news briefing.
"We will do as much as we can to provide infrastructure and supply and then prices will adjust to a lower level," he said, noting that supply was flat in 1997.
"The worst will soon be over," Wong said.
Hong Kong's property stocks roared on Friday as fears of draconian government measures to cool soaring prices ebbed.
Analysts have warned that Hong Kong needs to guard against a property "bubble" as prices climb ever higher.
They have also expressed concern that the new government led by Beijing-backed Tung Chee-hwa might slap a new capital gains tax on property sales to curb rampant speculation.

Wong stressed the present government had always operated in a very cautious way towards taxation of any kind, not just in the housing sector. He said the new government would have to carefully balance the pros and cons of imposing fresh taxes.
The incoming government's property advisor, C.Y. Leung, is drawing up proposals to address high housing costs in the tiny territory of 6.4 million people.
"Up to now I do not know what specific programmes Mr. C.Y. Leung will be recommending," Wong said.
As the future housing secretary, he said Leung would liaise with him, other colleagues and Tung Chee-hwa before a decision was taken.
Wong invited the private sector to help the government meet public housing targets and suggested that in return the private sector could benefit from streamlined building regulations.
"We now have a home ownership rate of 52 percent. It is our declared intention to encourage wider home ownership," he said.
